newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian miners fear further falls in gold price.
newsitem.headline: Australian miners fear further falls in gold price.

text.p: Australia's gold miners, still smarting from the sale of 167 tonnes of gold by the nation's central bank that sent bullion prices plummeting, said on Monday prices were likely to continue to fall and blamed the government.

Gold prices in the near-term should trade in the current range of US$320 to $325 an ounce after falling as low as $313 this month as the market begins absorbing the impact of the gold sales, the miners said.
Longer-term though, gold could be in for a further tumble as investors turn to other investments, they said.
"The RBA's (Reserve Bank of Australia) decision to sell gold has destroyed investor confidence in gold as a commodity," said Tony Gates, managing director of Capricorn Resources Australia NL.
"This means gold miners will face an inability to raise capital at home for exploration," Gates said.
The Australian Stock Exchange gold index, a measure of the health of the local gold industry, fell 16 percent after the RBA said it had sold 167 tonnes of gold, leaving only 80 tonnes in it vaults.
Australian mining houses typically turn to the share market for capital to fund exploration and expansions.

A Federal minister on Monday received only a lukewarm reception from Australia's legion of "junior" mining houses, attending the annual Diggers and Dealers mining conference in Kalgoorlie despite delivering an upbeat speech on government relations with miners.

Australian Minister for Resources and Energy, Warwick Parer, standing in for Prime Minister John Howard, who is ill, said it would be "improper" for the RBA to be ordered to buy back the gold sold by the central bank.
Some miners had hoped for a buy back by the bank as a sign of government support the mining industry.

For a growing number of mines the gold cash production costs, which do not take into account depreciation or amortisation expenses, are bordering on making some projects uneconomic to mine, the miners said.
"What the RBA did and how they did it was laughable," said Devex Ltd managing director Harry Adams.
Adams said he expects gold prices to trade lower for a while longer, eventually enticing investors back into the market and giving the metal a fillip.

The Association of Mining and Exploration Companies has called on the government to better study global financial markets and to try and "reverse the negative signals resulting from the debacle" surrounding the decision to sell off the gold.
Colin Patterson, managing director of Emperor Mines Ltd, which mines gold in Fiji, said "most of the damage from the gold sales had already been done."
Patterson said it would take about two years for the gold market to recover before showing signs of strenghtening.
"In the medium term, which I take to mean two years, I believe the price will rise," Patterson said.
